t: SpaceX plans up to 80,000 cell towers for Starlink Mobile, taking aim at America's biggest wireless carriers (Space Fans)
claim: SpaceX is reported (Bloomberg, 22-23 Oct 2026) to be in talks with tower companies for access to at least 80,000 US cell sites for a nationwide Starlink Mobile network - deals potentially worth billions. Own direct-to-device service targeted for early 2028 after a second-generation constellation deploys next year; also agreed to buy up to 14MHz of 800MHz spectrum from Grain Management (on top of the EchoStar spectrum).
x: Graded NOTED - TRUE, confirmed by Bloomberg via Mobile World Live; filed on Salee's instruction (24 Oct). CORRECTION ON RECORD: on 23 Oct Claude said the 80,000 figure was not confirmed - the search ran before the Bloomberg report surfaced. It is a CHANGE OF PLAN: in August SpaceX (Shotwell) said it would build on rooftops and Starlink dish sites and would not need many billions upfront; leasing 80,000 tower sites is the costlier, full fourth-carrier route. Crown Castle CEO: talking to all parties. AT&T: catching up takes a lot of years and huge investment. BOARD: SPCX stays WATCH-only (no budget) - loss-making under the rate rule, about 63x sales, vendor data unreliable until audited full-year numbers, and the mobile revenue arrives 2028, outside the near-term window. What is said here is arithmetic and sourcing only, for the NVDA holding (452 sh): (1) a $45bn six-year rental is about $7.5bn a year of compute, of which perhaps half to two thirds is the cost of NVIDIA systems - a few billion a year against NVIDIA data-centre revenue already above $150bn a year, i.e. low single digits of revenue; (2) it is Nscale, not Anthropic, that buys the GPUs, and Nscale must borrow to do so - the AI-compute debt-cost question raised on 10 Oct (Fed hike odds, 10-year above 5%) applies to it; (3) the chips are Vera Rubin, the generation AFTER Blackwell, deliveries from late 2027 - this is 2028 revenue for NVIDIA, not 2026; (4) per the 15 Sep standing note on compute-deal headlines, a reported figure is a ceiling of intent, not booked revenue, until a company reports it. t: Study Wealth (Thai) - Applied Materials: the company that benefits from five AI-chip bottlenecks (GAA, HBM, CoWoS/panel packaging, hybrid bonding, inspection)
claim: AMAT does not make the chips but sells the tools behind five hard steps: (1) GAA transistors need atomic-level deposition (Trillium ALD, Precision Selective Nitride, in use at 2nm and below); (2) HBM stacking needs CMP, ECD copper, PECVD stress films and eBeam defect review - new DRAM and packaging tools launched June 2026; (3) CoWoS and panel-level packaging - AMAT bought the NEXX business from ASMPT in 2026 for large-panel plating; (4) hybrid bonding - BESI joined the AMAT EPIC Center on 1 Oct 2026, raising switching costs; (5) inspection - VeritySEM 7AP and SEMVision G7AP. The writer notes AMAT does not break out revenue by technology, so the ~25% growth cannot be attributed to any one of these.
x: Graded NOTED - a well-argued post with its own caveats, and both dated claims check out against AMAT press releases (NEXX acquisition from ASMPT; Besi partnership expansion dated 1 Oct 2026). Nothing here changes a decision: we hold 57 AMAT at 19,702 cost, bought on exactly this picks-and-shovels logic, and the board already carries it at about +25% revenue growth. Two things I take from it: the Besi tie-up makes hybrid bonding a two-vendor process, which is good for lock-in and bad for anyone hoping AMAT does it alone; and the writer is right that the mix is undisclosed - the test that matters is the mid-November FQ4 print, where I will read the DRAM and advanced-packaging commentary, not the tech list. Not a reason to add before then.

t: TSMC outsources more CoWoS packaging - GlobalFoundries 2bn interposer deal (TrendForce)

x: 💡 TSMC keeps the expensive part and hands out the cheap parts - the 2-4nm compute dies (the high-margin work) stay in-house, while older-node interposers and assembly go to partners. That protects gross margin, which is exactly our 15 Oct TSMC test (buy 10,078 only at 65% or more). 📊 It also loosens the CoWoS bottleneck: more packaging capacity means more AI chips shipped by Nvidia and Broadcom (both owned). ⚠️ The GlobalFoundries fab only starts in 1H28 - this helps 2028, not 2026-27. Board: TSMC owned (147.5 sh); Amkor sold earlier; GlobalFoundries, UMC, ASE not on board (UMC and ASE are Taiwanese, allowed). 🎯 No new names; read TSMC 15 Oct results for CoWoS capacity and margin.

t: Humanoid robot anatomy — 12 components
claim: The 12 key parts that bring robots closer to humans
x: A clear teaching diagram with no companies, no prices and no numbers — nothing to act on. 💡 Worth keeping for one reason: the parts it names are where the money actually is. Actuators (3, 5, 10), sensors (1, 12), vision and the chest compute unit (4) are the high-value content; the frame, feet and battery case are commodity metalwork. Our only exposure sits in ISRG and CGNX — and Group 7 is still misnamed "Healthcare & Robotics" while holding no actuator or sensor maker at all.

t: "Intel CEO confirms memory crisis — prices up 5–7×"
claim: Memory prices up 5–7×, worst in 2027
x: True backwards, false forwards. ~5× is right for conventional DRAM contract prices over four quarters; 7× is unsupported. The quarterly rises go +93–98% → +58–63% → +13–18% — the acceleration is gone. NAND goes the other way in 2027; HBM never inflated at all. Intel sold its NAND business — it buys memory, it doesn't make it. Traces to one AI-translated Korean page. 🟡 Found an ambiguity in our own Micron condition with 12 days to run.

t: AI Cloud middle layer "eats the margin"
claim: The AI-cloud middleman collects the compute margin
x: Exactly backwards, and our own board proves it. Bottom (suppliers) NVDA +63.66%, MU +55.91%. Top (customers) MSFT +40.3%, GOOGL +37.9%. Middle: CRWV −25.4%, NBIS −32.7%, IREN −99.4% — every one loses money. 💡 Why it fools people: their gross margins are superb (67–77%). The money dies below the gross line — GPU depreciation and interest on the debt that bought them. We own none of the middle layer and banked +$1,074.73 exiting it.

t: Oracle invests in 1.7 GW of wind
claim: Not enough power for AI — Oracle invests 1.7 GW of wind
x: The number is right, the noun is wrong. These are power purchase agreements, not ownership — RWE's own release says "virtual power purchase agreement… for 433 megawatts" on wind farms commissioned in 2008 and 2009. Zero Oracle capex. Immaterial beside $28,499m of capex in one quarter and −$28.7bn trailing free cash flow. 🎯 Oracle is becoming the middle layer — the CoreWeave model at mega-cap scale. 💡 When a company says "invest", ask whether anything appears on its balance sheet.

t: OKLO "double bottom alert"
claim: Call setup / put setup off 4-hour, 1-hour and 15-minute charts
x: Not an investment slide — an options day-trading sheet. Its chart tops out at $52 while OKLO's all-time high is $193.84 — a window that excludes an 81% collapse, then prints "DOUBLE BOTTOM" in green. This board does not trade options.

t: Amazon–Generac deal
claim: An "$8 billion deal" between Amazon and Generac
x: The headline is wrong. The 8-K promises $2.4bn of expected deliveries; the $8bn is the level at which Amazon's warrant fully vests. That is 1.1% of Amazon's capex guide. 🎯 Third time in a month a supplier paid its customer in equity — after Google at TeraWulf and Cipher. Read the exhibit, not the headline.

t: 18 biotech names by theme
claim: "Money is flowing into biotech" — 18 names to watch
x: Interesting as a field, wrong for this board as built. Only 1 of 18 is ours (TEM, no budget). A clinical trial either works or it doesn't — a coin flip with a scientific prior, not volatility. The metric that decides survival is cash runway, and the slide gives it for zero of the eighteen. An AI-designed drug passes the same trials — AI can make you fail faster and cheaper; it cannot make biology work. 💡 The list is secretly two: tools (Illumina, Bruker, 10x, Twist, Natera) vs clinical-stage coin flips. 🟡 And it exposed that Group 7 is misnamed.

t: 7 defense & aerospace stocks
claim: LMT, NOC, GD, RTX, BA, PLTR, AXON benefit from a changing world
x: Yes defence is interesting — we already decided that, approved $35,000, and spent $5,700.88. Group 9 is the worst-deployed group on the board at 16.3%. And the allocation is backwards: LHX (+8.11% net margin) has $9,000 approved and ZERO invested; RKLB (−21.52%, ranked 80th of 81) holds the largest budget at $15,000. Only Palantir of the seven is ours. Fix the budget we have before adding a name.

t: Magnificent 7 cash
claim: Apple looks cash-poor next to its peers
x: Measured the wrong line. Apple holds $146,517m — second of the seven — because $84,118m sits in long-term marketable securities that cash charts drop. 💡 On net cash the ranking inverts and Amazon, the chart's №2, is $5.9bn in debt. The big piles are working capital for a construction programme, not trophies.

t: "11 stocks you haven't missed yet"
claim: Eleven stocks still early enough to buy
x: The worst-made slide yet. SEZL appears twice; Nebius is given Pat Gelsinger as CEO; IREN is labelled "$REN"; AppLovin carries an Apple logo; Micron carries an AMD logo. And every price on it is below the market — a list titled "stocks you haven't missed" has already missed them.

t: PEG ratio / Lumentum
claim: A PEG of 0.32 makes it cheap
x: PEG is the weakest number on any slide. Separately, LITE's −230% net margin proved real — a $7,756.6m non-cash loss on settling convertible notes, while free cash flow was +$300.1m. 💡 An implausible number is not necessarily a wrong number.

t: Eight biggest pullbacks from all-time high
claim: Stocks far below their highs = opportunity
x: Reviewed name by name; no position changes. A large fall is a fact about the price, not a fact about the business.

t: Humanoid robots (Musk 1bn / XPeng 10 min)
claim: One billion humanoids within ten years
x: Vocabulary added to the dictionary — takt time, nameplate capacity, pre-orders vs shipments, disclosed vs asserted. No position changes.
